newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Court says Germany exposed to tourist liability suits.
newsitem.headline: Court says Germany exposed to tourist liability suits.

text.p: The European Court of Justice said on Tuesday Germany's failure to transpose EU law protecting tourists exposed it to liablility suits from German travellers.
The court said that a member state's failure to transpose a directive within the time required was a per se serious breach of Community law which gives rise to liability.
Council of Ministers Directive 90/314/EEC requires tour operators to provide guarantees to their package tourist clients to protect them in the event of business failure.

The directive required Germany to enact the EU rules no later than December, 1992. In June 1994, Germany did enact the travel directive, adding a new provision which prevented tour operators from taking funds from travellers until a document of security was provided to the traveller.

After package tour purchasers were stranded or unable to travel in 1993 because their tour operators went bankrupt, they initiated lawsuits against Germany saying that if the travel directive had been adopted, they would have been protected.

The court reaffirmed its reasoning of earlier rulings in Francovich (C-6/90 and C-9/90), Factortame (C-48/93) Brasserie du Pecheur (C-46/93) and British Telecommunications (C-393/93) that a serious breach by member states of a clearly defined individual right under EU law, which causes harm to an individual, gives rise to liability suits against member states by those individuals.

The German court will now decide the issue of damages but the European court has rejected the German government's argument that airline tickets or hotel vouchers provide sufficient security against a bankrupt travel agency.

The court found consumer protection guarantees under the travel directive could be impaired if travelers were required to enforce credit vouchers against third parties who might also be creditors of the bankrupt travel agency.
EXCERPTS FROM THE JUDGMENT
(Court translation into English. Original language of the case: German)
"Directive 90/314/EEC on package travel, package holidays and package tours - Non-transportation - Liability of the member state and its obligation to make reparation"
Reference to the court from the Landgericht (Regional Court) Bonn for a preliminary ruling in the proceedings pending before that court between
Erich Dillenkoffer
Christian Erdmann
Hans-Jurgen Schulte
Anke Heuer
Werner, Ursula and Torsten Know
and
Federal Republic of Germany
on the interpretation of Council directive 90/314/EEC of 13 June 1990 on package travel, package holidays and package tours (OJ 1990 L 158, p. 59)
THE COURT hereby rules

1. Failure to take any measure to transpose a directive in order to achieve the result it prescribes within the period laid down for that purpose constitues per se a serious breach of Community law and consequently gives rise to a right of reparation for individuals suffering injury if the result prescribed by the directive entails the grant to individuals of rights whose content is identifiable and a causal link exists between the breach of the state's obligation and the loss and damgage suffered.

2. The result prescribed by article 7 of Council directive 90/314/EEC of 13 June 1990 on package travel, package holidays and package tours entails the grant to package travellers of rights guaranteeing a refund of money paid over and their repatriation in the event of the organizer's insolvency; the content of those rights is sufficiently identifiable.

3. In order to comply with article 9 of directive 90/314, the member state should have adopted, within the period prescribed, all the measures necessary to ensure that, as from January 1 1993, individuals would have effective protection againt the risk of the insolvency of the organizer and/or retailer party to the contract.

4. If a member state allows the package travel organizer and/or retailer party to a contract to require payment of a deposit of up to 10 percent towards the travel price, with a maximum of DM 500, the protective purpose pursued by article 7 of directive 90/314 is not satisfied unless a refund of that deposit is also guaranteed in the event of the insolvency of the package travel organizer and/or retailer to the contract.

5. Article 7 of directive 90/314 is to be interpreted as meaning that the 'security' of which organizers must offer sufficient eveidence is lacking even if, on payment of the travel price, travellers are in possession of documents of value and that the Federal Republic of Germany could not have omitted altogether to transpose directive 90/314 on the basis of the Bundesgerichtshof's advance payment' judgment of 12 March 1987.
6. Direcive 90/314 does not require member states to adopt sepcific measures in relation to article 7 in order to protect package travellers against their own negligence.
